questions.q: A student writes: "Current I = 5 C flowing through a wire." Identify the error and state the correct quantity with its unit.
questions.a: Error: Current is a rate, not an amount of charge. The student confused charge (Q, unit coulomb) with current (I, unit ampere = C/s). Correct statement: "Current I = 5 A" or "Charge Q = 5 C passed in 1 s." This reveals the student does not grasp the "per unit time" in the definition.

questions.q: In a copper wire, electrons drift from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of a battery. What is the direction of conventional current? Why was this convention chosen historically?
questions.a: Conventional current direction is from positive terminal to negative terminal outside the battery (opposite to electron drift). The convention was established before the discovery of the electron; early scientists assumed positive charges moved. It is retained for consistency in circuit analysis. A wrong answer (e.g., "same as electron flow") shows the student memorizes direction without understanding the historical convention.

questions.q: A steady current of 2.5 A flows through a household fan motor for 10 minutes. Calculate the total charge that passes through any cross-section of the wire. Express in coulombs.
questions.a: Given: I = 2.5 A, t = 10 min = 600 s. Using I = Q/t → Q = I × t = 2.5 A × 600 s = 1500 C. Steps: (1) convert time to seconds, (2) multiply current by time, (3) check unit: A·s = C. A wrong answer like 25 C (using 10 instead of 600) reveals failure to convert minutes to seconds.

questions.q: Two wires A and B carry currents 3 A and 5 A respectively. Wire A has electrons drifting at 0.2 mm/s; wire B has electrons drifting at 0.1 mm/s. Which wire has higher charge carrier density n (assuming same cross-sectional area and charge per carrier)? Justify using I = nAev_d.
questions.a: From I = nAev_d, n ∝ I/v_d (since A, e constant). For wire A: n_A ∝ 3/0.2 = 15. For wire B: n_B ∝ 5/0.1 = 50. Thus n_B > n_A. Wire B has higher carrier density. A student who picks wire A because "higher drift speed means more charge" confuses drift speed with current magnitude.

questions.q: A student solves a circuit problem and writes: "Current entering junction = 3 A, leaving = 2 A + 2 A = 4 A. Since 3 ≠ 4, Kirchhoff's junction rule is violated, so the problem is wrong." Evaluate this reasoning.
questions.a: The student's reasoning is flawed. Kirchhoff's junction rule is a law of nature (conservation of charge), not a condition that can be "violated" in a real circuit. If the numbers don't add up, the student's assumed current values or directions are incorrect, not the rule. The correct approach: assign unknown currents with arrows, apply junction rule to get equations, then solve. This error shows the student treats the rule as a check rather than a solving tool.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a battery, an ammeter, a variable resistor, and a stopwatch to verify that current is the rate of flow of charge. Describe the procedure, measurements, and how you would calculate charge from current readings.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Connect battery, ammeter, and variable resistor in series. (2) Set resistor to a value, close switch, start stopwatch. (3) Record steady current I at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 s) for 1 minute. (4) Open switch. (5) Plot I vs t; if constant, area under graph = I × Δt = Q. (6) Repeat for different resistor values. A good answer includes: constant current assumption, area under I-t graph gives charge, unit consistency (A·s = C). A poor answer measures only one current value and multiplies by total time without verifying steadiness.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Electric current is the rate of flow of net charge across a cross-______ area of a conductor.
Fill in the blank: Observe a mobile phone charging: the battery icon shows a ______ bolt, indicating charge flow.
What is Electric current? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Electric current is the rate of flow of net charge across a cross-sectional area of a conductor.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Electric current?
questions.a: Students think "current is a vector because it has direction (arrow in circuit diagrams)." They incorrectly apply vector addition (parallelogram law) to currents at a junction.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) calculate current from given charge and time data with correct units, (2) distinguish between conventional current direction and electron drift direction in a metal, and (3) explain why current is a scalar despite being represented with an arrow in circuit diagrams.
